steps.body:
Welcome back. You can write functions now, which means you can build real tools. Today you get a container to build them around.

So far each variable holds ONE value. A list holds many, in order. You make one with square brackets and commas: scores = [90, 85, 72]. Now a single name holds the whole collection.

You reach one item by its position, its index, in square brackets. Here is the rule that catches everyone (you already met it as IndexError): positions start at 0. So scores[0] is the first item, 90, and scores[1] is the second, 85. Two more handies: a negative index counts from the end, so scores[-1] is always the LAST item however long the list is, and len(scores) tells you how many items are in it.

steps.prompt: Run this. First item, last item, and how many.
Positions start at 0, so position 1 is the SECOND item. What prints?

steps.body:
You can grab a whole SLICE (a sub-list) with two positions: items[1:3] gives you positions 1 and 2. Notice it stops BEFORE the second number, exactly like range did. Shortcuts: items[:2] is the first two, and items[2:] is from position 2 to the end.

The natural partner of a list is the for loop. for score in scores: walks every item in order, handing you one at a time, no indexing required. This is the everyday way to work through a list: loop over it and do something with each item. Combine that with the accumulator you learned, and you can total, count, or collect anything.

steps.prompt: Run this. A slice, then a walk through every item.
steps.code:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(nums[1:3])
for n in nums:
    print(n)

steps.prompt: items[:2] means from the start up to (but not including) position 2. Python prints a list with square brackets and quotes around text. What prints exactly?
Loop and accumulate, the same pattern from Module 5, now over a list. What prints?
steps.code:
prices = [4, 6, 10]
total = 0
for p in prices:
    total += p
print(total)

reviewForm.prompt: Total the list [4, 6, 10] with a loop. What prints?
reviewForm.code:

total = 0
for p in prices:
    total += p
print(total)

steps.body:
Lists come with built-in verbs, called methods, that you call with a dot. The big ones:
.append(x) adds x to the end. This is the workhorse.
.remove(x) deletes the first x it finds.
.sort() puts the items in order, low to high or alphabetical.

And two built-in helpers that TAKE a list: sum(numbers) adds them all up, and max(numbers) finds the biggest.

append is the one you will lean on most. Start with an empty list, [], then loop and append to collect results as you go. That is the list version of the accumulator: instead of adding to a number, you are building up a list.

steps.prompt: Run this. Start empty, append twice, check the result and the length.
steps.code:
todo = []
todo.append("wash car")
todo.append("call mom")
print(todo)
print(len(todo))

steps.prompt: .sort() reorders the list in place, smallest first. What prints?
Drag these into order to build a new list holding only the numbers bigger than 5. Start with an empty list, walk the numbers, and append the ones that pass. Watch the two levels of indentation.

reviewForm.prompt: To collect only some items from a list into a new list, what three ingredients do you need?
reviewForm.expected: An empty list to start, a for loop to walk the items, and an if inside that appends only the ones that pass.

steps.body:
Here is the surprise that trips up nearly everyone. Understanding it will save you hours of head-scratching.

A list is MUTABLE: you can change its contents in place, after it is made. You can overwrite an item by its position (nums[0] = 99) or grow the list with append. Numbers and strings are not like that; a list is. That flexibility hides a catch.

When you write b = a and a is a list, you do NOT get a copy. Both names now point at the SAME list, like two labels stuck on one box. So if you change the list through b, the change shows up through a too, because there is only one list underneath. This sharing is called aliasing.

If you truly want a separate copy, ask for one: b = a.copy(). Then they are two independent boxes. Any time a change to one list mysteriously appears in another, aliasing is almost always the reason.

steps.prompt: This is the classic surprise. b = a does NOT copy. We change the list through b, then print a. What prints?

reviewForm.prompt: a = [1, 2, 3]; b = a; b.append(4). What does print(a) show?

steps.prompt: You write b = a where a is a list, then b.append(9). Which statement is true?
choices: a and b point at the same list, so a now ends with 9 too.
b changes but a is untouched, because b is a copy.

reviewForm.prompt: b = a (both lists), then b.append(9). Does a change?
reviewForm.expected: Yes. b = a does not copy; both names point at the same list, so appending through b changes a too.

steps.prompt: Trace the list as it changes in place: append 15 to the end, then overwrite position 0 with a new value. What prints?

reviewForm.prompt: Trace it: nums = [5, 10]; append 15; set nums[0] = 0. What prints?

steps.body: Two moves show up in almost every program that touches data: FILTER (keep only the items that match a rule) and SUMMARIZE (boil a list down to one number, like a total or an average). You already have every piece: a loop, an if, an empty list to append into, and functions to wrap it all up. Let us put them together.

steps.starterCode:
def only_positive(nums):

    result = []

    return result

steps.prompt: Teach it back to the rubber duck: explain, in plain words, why writing b = a (where a is a list) does not give you a safe copy. What is the mental picture (hint: two labels, one box), and how do you get a real copy when you need one?

boss.name: The Data Sieve
boss.taunt: A month of numbers. Sift out what matters and tell me the story in one figure.
boss.brief:
Real data work is two moves: filter out what you care about, then summarize it. You get a list of daily step counts and you build both tools.

Write two functions:

1. high_scorers(steps, cutoff): return a NEW list holding only the days at or above the cutoff (use >=). Filter.

2. average(steps): return the average of the list, rounded to 2 decimals. Summarize. IMPORTANT: if the list is empty, return 0.0 rather than crashing on a divide by zero. (sum(steps) adds a list up, len(steps) counts it.)

Worked example: high_scorers([5000, 8000, 12000, 7000], 7500) is [8000, 12000] (only the days that met the bar). average([5000, 8000, 12000, 7000]) is 8000.0.

This is everything from the module: lists, iteration, a condition, append, and a careful check for the empty case.

hiddenTests.message: keep only the days at or above 7500, which are 8000 and 12000
when no day meets the cutoff, return an empty list
the cutoff is inclusive, so a day exactly at 7500 counts (use >=)
the average of those four days is 8000.0
an empty list should return 0.0, so guard against dividing by a length of zero

terms.definition: An ordered container that holds many values: [90, 85, 72]. Reach an item by its index (positions start at 0), and len() tells you how many.
A position in a list, counted from 0. items[0] is the first, items[-1] is the last. Asking for a position that does not exist is an IndexError.
A sub-list grabbed with two positions: items[1:3] gives positions 1 and 2. It stops before the second number, like range.
Adds an item to the end of a list. The workhorse for building a list up: start with [] and append inside a loop.
Able to be changed in place after it is made. Lists are mutable; numbers and strings are not. This is what makes append and item assignment possible.
When two names point at the SAME list, so a change through one shows up through the other. b = a shares the list; b = a.copy() makes a separate one.
